hypotheses.title: Anyone can call finalizeRequestManual to finalize any account's withdraw request
hypotheses.description: `finalizeRequestManual` has no access control modifier (no `onlyApprovedVault`, no `onlyOwner`). Any external caller can finalize any vault/account's pending withdraw request. The function calls `_finalizeWithdraw` which sets `s.finalized = true` and `s.totalWithdraw` on the tokenized request, locking in the withdraw amount for all tokenized shares.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a pending withdraw request for a victim vault/account. 2. Attacker calls `finalizeRequestManual(vault, account)` directly. 3. The request is finalized and `s_tokenizedWithdrawRequest[requestId].finalized = true` with `totalWithdraw` set. 4. Any subsequent legitimate finalization path returns the cached value; the attacker can time this to force finalization at an unfavorable moment (e.g., before yield accrues or during a manipulation window), or to grief the vault's accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized state transition on victim withdraw requests; griefing and potential value loss if finalization is forced at an attacker-chosen time.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyApprovedVault` (or restrict to the owning vault) to `finalizeRequestManual`.

hypotheses.title: Chainlink oracle round staleness/answeredInRound not validated in custom oracles
hypotheses.description: `_calculateBaseToQuote` reads `baseToUSDOracle.latestRoundData()` and only checks `baseToUSD > 0`. It never validates `updatedAt` freshness, `answeredInRound >= roundId`, or `startedAt != 0`. The same pattern exists in `PendlePTOracle._calculateBaseToQuote`. A stale or incomplete Chainlink round will be accepted and used to price LP/PT tokens, which feeds `AbstractYieldStrategy.price()` and Morpho collateral valuation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Wait for the underlying Chainlink feed to become stale (heartbeat missed / L2 outage) or for a round where `answeredInRound < roundId`. 2) The oracle still returns the last answer. 3) Attacker opens a Morpho position or liquidates using the stale price, borrowing against inflated collateral or seizing collateral cheaply.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong collateral valuation → over-borrowing / under-collateralized debt, or unfair liquidations; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `updatedAt != 0`, `block.timestamp - updatedAt <= heartbeat`, and `answeredInRound >= roundId` before using the answer.

hypotheses.title: Morpho flash loan callback lacks initiator authentication
hypotheses.description: `onMorphoFlashLoan` only checks `msg.sender == address(MORPHO)`, but Morpho's `flashLoan` is a permissionless entry point that any external caller can invoke with arbitrary `data`. The callback decodes `onBehalf`, `vault`, `asset`, `depositAssetAmount`, `depositData`, and `migrateFrom` entirely from attacker-supplied `data` and then performs `_enterOrMigrate` and `MORPHO.borrow` on behalf of `onBehalf`. There is no check that the flash loan was initiated by this router (e.g. no transient flag set in `_flashBorrowAndEnter`), so any caller can drive the router's privileged internal logic.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `MORPHO.flashLoan(asset, amount, craftedData)` directly. 2) Morpho calls `onMorphoLendingRouter.onMorphoFlashLoan(assets, craftedData)`. 3) Router decodes attacker-chosen `onBehalf`/`vault`/`migrateFrom` and executes `_enterOrMigrate` (which can call `mintShares` on a vault, or `exitPosition` on a previous lending router via `migrateFrom`) and then `MORPHO.borrow(m, assets, 0, onBehalf, address(this))`. 4) Attacker repays the flash loan from the borrowed funds and keeps any residual value, or forces a victim's position to be opened/migrated without consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized position creation/migration on behalf of arbitrary accounts, unauthorized borrowing against victim collateral, and potential theft of vault shares or borrowed assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set a transient flag in `_flashBorrowAndEnter` before calling `MORPHO.flashLoan` and require it to be set (and clear it) in `onMorphoFlashLoan`; also bind the callback to the exact parameters passed in.

hypotheses.title: Dinero canFinalizeWithdrawRequest returns true when outstandingRedemptions <= totalAssets
hypotheses.description: The final check is `return PirexETH.outstandingRedemptions() > totalAssets;`. The comment says "Can only finalize if the total assets are greater than the outstanding redemptions", which is the opposite of the code. As written, the function returns true only when `outstandingRedemptions > totalAssets`, i.e. when the protocol still owes more than it has, which is exactly when redemption should NOT be allowed. Conversely, when the protocol has enough assets to cover redemptions (`outstandingRedemptions <= totalAssets`), the function returns false and finalization is blocked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (approved vault) initiates a Dinero withdraw request. 2) Once validators are dissolved/slashed and `outstandingRedemptions <= totalAssets`, the attacker calls `finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest`. 3) `canFinalizeWithdrawRequest` returns false, so `_finalizeWithdrawImpl` returns `finalized = false` and no tokens are claimed. 4) The attacker cannot finalize even though the protocol is solvent, and the request is stuck. 5) Conversely, when `outstandingRedemptions > totalAssets` (insolvent), the function returns true and the attacker can finalize, potentially draining upxETH that should be reserved for other redeemers.
hypotheses.impact: Withdraw requests are permanently stuck when the protocol is solvent, and can be drained when the protocol is insolvent, causing loss of funds for other redeemers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Invert the condition to `return PirexETH.outstandingRedemptions() <= totalAssets;` to match the comment and the intended solvency check.

hypotheses.title: Curve LP oracle spot price check uses manipulable get_dy without TWAP
hypotheses.description: `_lpTokenValue` computes `spotPrices[SECONDARY_INDEX]` via `ICurvePool(LP_TOKEN).get_dy(...)` — a single-block spot quote — and `AbstractLPOracle._calculateLPTokenValue` only checks that this spot price is within `LOWER/UPPER_LIMIT_MULTIPLIER` of the oracle pair price. An attacker who can move the Curve pool spot price within the tolerance band (or push it just inside the band) can skew the LP valuation, since the LP value is derived from `balances[i]` which are also manipulable via a flash loan into the pool.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Flash-borrow large amount of one pool token. 2) Swap into the Curve pool to shift `balances` and `get_dy` spot price. 3) Call a function that reads `Curve2TokenOracle.latestRoundData()` (e.g., Morpho `healthFactor`/`liquidate` or vault `price()`). 4) Exploit inflated/deflated LP value to borrow more or liquidate at a discount. 5) Reverse swap and repay flash loan.
hypotheses.impact: Over-borrowing against manipulated collateral, or discounted liquidation of victim positions; loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a TWAP or time-weighted balance for both `balances` and the spot check, or tighten tolerance and require multi-block observation.

hypotheses.title: AbstractRewardManager.updateAccountRewards can be called by anyone via fallback
hypotheses.description: The fallback in `RewardManagerMixin` delegates any call to `REWARD_MANAGER` except for `updateAccountRewards`. However, `AbstractRewardManager.updateAccountRewards` is declared `external` with no access control, and the fallback only blocks the exact selector `IRewardManager.updateAccountRewards.selector`. An attacker can call `updateAccountRewards` directly on the reward manager (not through the vault) with arbitrary `account`, `effectiveSupplyBefore`, `accountSharesBefore`, `accountSharesAfter`, and `sharesInEscrow` values. This lets the attacker manipulate `_getAccountRewardDebtSlot()[rewardToken][account]` and `_getVaultRewardStateSlot()` accumulators, inflating or zeroing reward debt for any account.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `AbstractRewardManager.updateAccountRewards(victim, hugeEffectiveSupply, 0, hugeSharesAfter, false)` directly on the reward manager. 2) The function calls `_claimVaultRewards` and then `_claimRewardToken` for each reward token, setting `rewardDebt[victim] = accountSharesAfter * rewardsPerVaultShare / DEFAULT_PRECISION`. 3) Attacker sets `accountSharesAfter` to a huge value, making `rewardDebt[victim]` huge. 4) When the victim later claims through the vault, `rewardToClaim = accountSharesBefore * rewardsPerVaultShare / DEFAULT_PRECISION - rewardDebt` underflows or is zero, so the victim receives nothing. 5) Attacker can also set `accountSharesAfter = 0` to zero out the debt and then claim the victim's accrued rewards via a subsequent call.
hypotheses.impact: Any account's reward debt can be arbitrarily manipulated, causing loss of accrued rewards for victims and potentially draining the reward manager's reward token balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an access control check to `updateAccountRewards` (e.g., only callable by the vault via delegatecall) or remove it from the public ABI and only expose it through the vault's internal `_updateAccountRewards`.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor inflation attack via virtual shares offset
hypotheses.description: The vault uses VIRTUAL_SHARES = 1e6 and VIRTUAL_YIELD_TOKENS = 1, which is a very small virtual offset relative to typical ERC4626 mitigations. An attacker can be the first depositor, mint a tiny amount of shares, then donate yield tokens directly to the vault to inflate the share price, causing subsequent depositors to receive zero or near-zero shares due to rounding down in `convertYieldTokenToShares`. The `_mintSharesGivenAssets` computes `sharesMinted = (yieldTokensMinted * effectiveSupply()) / (initialYieldTokenBalance - feesAccrued() + VIRTUAL_YIELD_TOKENS)` which rounds down and can be zero for small deposits after donation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is first depositor, mints 1 wei of shares via mintShares with 1 wei asset. 2) Attacker transfers a large amount of yieldToken directly to the vault address (donation). 3) Victim calls mintShares with a normal deposit; `initialYieldTokenBalance` is now huge, so `sharesMinted = yieldTokensMinted * effectiveSupply / (huge balance)` rounds down to 0. 4) Victim receives 0 shares but their assets are transferred into the vault, benefiting the attacker who can redeem the inflated shares.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds for subsequent depositors; attacker can steal deposits via share price manipulation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a much larger virtual offset (e.g., 1e18 virtual shares) or implement a dead-shares mechanism on first deposit to prevent donation-based inflation.

hypotheses.title: getWithdrawRequestValue divides by sharesAmount without zero check
hypotheses.description: `getWithdrawRequestValue` returns `totalValue * shares / w.sharesAmount` at the end. If `w.sharesAmount` is zero (which can happen if a withdraw request was created with sharesAmount=0, or if all shares were tokenized away leaving a zero sharesAmount but non-zero requestId), this division reverts. The `initiateWithdraw` function does not validate `sharesAmount > 0`, and `tokenizeWithdrawRequest` can reduce `s_withdraw.sharesAmount` to zero only in the full-transfer branch which deletes the request, but partial tokenization could theoretically leave dust. More importantly, `initiateWithdraw` accepts `sharesAmount = 0` from an approved vault.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An approved vault (or a bug in a vault) calls `initiateWithdraw` with `sharesAmount = 0` and some `yieldTokenAmount`. 2) The request is stored with `sharesAmount = 0`. 3) Any call to `getWithdrawRequestValue` for that account reverts due to division by zero, bricking valuation and potentially DoS-ing the vault's health factor calculations.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on valuation; vault positions become unvaluable, potentially freezing funds.

hypotheses.title: AbstractCustomOracle.latestAnswer/latestTimestamp skip sequencer check
hypotheses.description: `latestRoundData()` calls `_checkSequencer()`, but `latestAnswer()`, `latestTimestamp()`, and `latestRound()` call `_calculateBaseToQuote()` directly without `_checkSequencer()`. Any consumer using these legacy AggregatorV2V3 methods (common in integrations) will receive prices while the L2 sequencer is down or within the grace period, defeating the sequencer protection.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Sequencer goes down on the L2. 2) Attacker (or any integration) calls `latestAnswer()` on the custom oracle, which returns a price despite the outage. 3) Uses that price to enter/liquidate positions before the sequencer recovers and prices update.
hypotheses.impact: Stale/incorrect pricing during sequencer downtime → unfair liquidations or over-borrowing.

hypotheses.title: EtherFi finalize uses ownerOf check that reverts on burned NFT
hypotheses.description: `canFinalizeWithdrawRequest` calls `WithdrawRequestNFT.ownerOf(requestId) != address(0)`. For ERC721, `ownerOf` reverts when the token does not exist (e.g. after `claimWithdraw` burns the NFT). If a request has already been claimed (or the NFT was burned for any reason), `canFinalizeWithdrawRequest` reverts instead of returning false, which propagates up through `_finalizeWithdrawImpl` and `finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest`, bricking the finalization path for that request.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A withdraw request is finalized and claimed via `claimWithdraw`, burning the NFT. 2) Any subsequent call to `finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest` for that request (e.g. a partial redemption or a retry) calls `canFinalizeWithdrawRequest`, which calls `ownerOf` on a burned token and reverts. 3) The account's withdraw request cannot be finalized or redeemed, and the vault's `_finalizeWithdraw` path reverts, freezing the account's shares and the vault's accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds: the account's withdraw request cannot be finalized, and the vault's `finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest` reverts, blocking redemptions and potentially locking the vault's yield tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `ownerOf(requestId) != address(0)` with a try/catch or use `WithdrawRequestNFT.isFinalized(requestId)` alone, and handle the burned-NFT case by returning false.

hypotheses.title: Liquidator can claim rewards on shares they never held via pre/post liquidation accounting
hypotheses.description: In `_postLiquidation`, the liquidator's reward debt is updated using `t_Liquidator_SharesBefore` (their native balance captured in `_preLiquidation`) as `accountSharesBefore`, and `t_Liquidator_SharesBefore + sharesToLiquidator` as `accountSharesAfter`. However, the liquidator's shares are transferred to them *after* this accounting via `postLiquidation`'s `_transfer`. The reward debt is set to `(accountSharesAfter * rewardsPerVaultShare)`, meaning the liquidator is credited as if they held `sharesToLiquidator` for the entire period since the last accumulation, even though they only just received them. Meanwhile the liquidateAccount is debited from `t_LiquidateAccount_SharesBefore` down to `t_LiquidateAccount_SharesBefore - sharesToLiquidator`, so the shares are effectively double-counted in the reward accumulator for the current period.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a liquidatable position. 2) Attacker calls `liquidate()` on the lending router with `sharesToLiquidate` equal to the full collateral. 3) In `_postLiquidation`, the liquidator's reward debt is set based on `sharesBefore + sharesToLiquidator` while the liquidateAccount's debt is reduced by the same amount — but the accumulator `accumulatedRewardPerVaultShare` was already advanced using `effectiveSupplyBefore` which still includes the liquidateAccount's shares. 4) The liquidator can then call `claimAccountRewards` (or the next reward accrual) and receive rewards for shares they held for zero time, while the liquidateAccount loses the rewards they legitimately accrued.
hypotheses.impact: Reward tokens are over-distributed to liquidators at the expense of the protocol's reward pool and honest holders; repeated liquidations drain reward balances and cause later claimants to receive less than owed (or transfers to fail silently, emitting zero).
hypotheses.recommendation: Update the liquidator's reward debt using `accountSharesBefore = t_Liquidator_SharesBefore` and `accountSharesAfter = t_Liquidator_SharesBefore` (i.e., claim only what they had before), then set the new debt after the transfer; or perform the reward update after the share transfer so `balanceOf` reflects reality.

hypotheses.title: finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest partial-withdraw math uses stale totalWithdraw
hypotheses.description: When a withdraw request is finalized, `_finalizeWithdraw` computes `tokensWithdrawn` as `s.totalWithdraw * w.yieldTokenAmount / s.totalYieldTokenAmount`. In the partial-withdraw branch, the code then rescales this already-scaled value again by `withdrawYieldTokenAmount / s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount`. Because `w.yieldTokenAmount` is the account's share of the tokenized request, the second scaling double-counts the tokenization ratio, so the vault receives fewer tokens than it should. The same double-scaling also corrupts the subsequent `s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount` decrement, leaving the account's remaining claim inconsistent with the tokenized request's `totalYieldTokenAmount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (approved vault) initiates a withdraw request for account A with yieldTokenAmount Y. 2) A second account B tokenizes part of the request, so `s.totalYieldTokenAmount` stays Y but A's `w.yieldTokenAmount` is reduced to Y'. 3) Attacker calls `finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest(A, withdrawYieldTokenAmount = Y', sharesToBurn = sharesA)` — the partial branch triggers because Y' < Y. 4) `tokensWithdrawn` is computed as `totalWithdraw * Y' / Y` and then multiplied again by `Y' / Y'`, i.e. it is not rescaled at all, but the storage decrement `s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount -= Y'` leaves A with zero claim while the tokenized request still holds `totalYieldTokenAmount = Y`. 5) Attacker repeats for B, draining more than the request's actual `totalWithdraw`.
hypotheses.impact: Vaults can withdraw more than the finalized request's `totalWithdraw`, draining the withdraw request manager's WITHDRAW_TOKEN balance and leaving later redeemers unable to claim. Accounting for remaining yield tokens is permanently corrupted.
hypotheses.recommendation: In the partial branch, do not rescale `tokensWithdrawn` again — `_finalizeWithdraw` already returns the account's pro-rata share. Instead compute `tokensWithdrawn = tokensWithdrawn * withdrawYieldTokenAmount / w.yieldTokenAmount` only when `_finalizeWithdraw` returned the raw `totalWithdraw`, or restructure so the tokenization ratio is applied exactly once.

hypotheses.title: Partial finalize in finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest can leave inconsistent state
hypotheses.description: When `withdrawYieldTokenAmount < s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount`, the function computes `tokensWithdrawn = tokensWithdrawn * withdrawYieldTokenAmount / s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount` and then decrements `s_withdraw.sharesAmount` and `s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount`. However, the tokenized request's `totalYieldTokenAmount` and `totalWithdraw` are not updated, so subsequent calls to `_finalizeWithdraw` for other accounts sharing the same requestId will use stale totals. This causes the proportional claim calculation `totalWithdraw * w.yieldTokenAmount / totalYieldTokenAmount` to be inconsistent with the actual remaining tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Two accounts share a tokenized withdraw request (via tokenizeWithdrawRequest). 2) Account A partially finalizes, reducing their `yieldTokenAmount` but not the tokenized totals. 3) Account B finalizes and receives a payout computed against the original `totalWithdraw` and `totalYieldTokenAmount`, which no longer reflect the actual remaining tokens. 4) Account B can receive more than their fair share, draining tokens from the manager.
hypotheses.impact: Over-payment to later withdrawers; insolvency of the withdraw request manager for remaining accounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `s_tokenizedWithdrawRequest[requestId].totalYieldTokenAmount` and `totalWithdraw` proportionally when partial finalization occurs, or disallow partial finalization on tokenized requests.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in initiateWithdraw via _initiateWithdrawImpl external calls
hypotheses.description: In `initiateWithdraw`, the function first checks `accountWithdraw.requestId != 0` to prevent existing requests, then transfers YIELD_TOKEN from the vault, then calls `_initiateWithdrawImpl` (which for Ethena clones a holder and calls `holder.startCooldown`, for EtherFi calls `weETH.unwrap` and `LiquidityPool.requestWithdraw`, etc.), and only AFTER that sets `accountWithdraw.requestId = requestId`. During the external call in `_initiateWithdrawImpl`, the attacker can reenter `initiateWithdraw` for the same account since `accountWithdraw.requestId` is still 0. This allows creating multiple withdraw requests for the same account, each transferring YIELD_TOKEN from the vault.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is an approved vault. 2) Attacker calls `initiateWithdraw(account, yieldTokenAmount, sharesAmount, data)` where `data` triggers an external call that reenters (e.g., a malicious token or a callback in the withdraw manager implementation). 3) During `_initiateWithdrawImpl`, the attacker reenters `initiateWithdraw` for the same `account`. 4) The check `accountWithdraw.requestId != 0` passes because it hasn't been set yet. 5) A second withdraw request is created, and the vault's YIELD_TOKEN is transferred again.
hypotheses.impact: Multiple withdraw requests for the same account, each backed by the same shares, leading to double-counting of yield tokens and potential loss of funds when finalizing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `accountWithdraw.requestId` and other state before calling `_initiateWithdrawImpl`, or add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: tokenizeWithdrawRequest allows overwriting _to's yieldTokenAmount without checking requestId match
hypotheses.description: The function checks `toWithdraw.requestId != 0 && toWithdraw.requestId != requestId` and reverts, but when `toWithdraw.requestId == requestId` it proceeds to add `s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount` to `toWithdraw.yieldTokenAmount`. If `_to` already had a request with the same `requestId` (which can happen because `requestId` is derived from the holder address in Ethena or from a counter in Generic managers), the addition is legitimate. However, in the `s_withdraw.sharesAmount == sharesAmount` branch the code adds `s_withdraw.yieldTokenAmount` to `toWithdraw.yieldTokenAmount` and then deletes `_from`'s request — but `toWithdraw.yieldTokenAmount` was never validated against `s_tokenizedWithdrawRequest[requestId].totalYieldTokenAmount`. A malicious approved vault can call `tokenizeWithdrawRequest` repeatedly with the same `_from`/`_to` pair after `_from` has been deleted, or with a `_to` whose requestId matches but whose yieldTokenAmount was previously inflated, causing the tokenized request's per-account claims to exceed `totalYieldTokenAmount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Approved vault V calls `initiateWithdraw(A, Y, S, data)` → requestId R, `s_tokenizedWithdrawRequest[R].totalYieldTokenAmount = Y`. 2) V calls `tokenizeWithdrawRequest(A, B, S)` → B gets `yieldTokenAmount = Y`, A deleted. 3) V calls `tokenizeWithdrawRequest(B, C, S)` → C gets `yieldTokenAmount = Y`. 4) V calls `tokenizeWithdrawRequest(C, B, S)` → B's requestId is still R, so the check passes and B's `yieldTokenAmount` becomes `Y + Y = 2Y`. 5) V calls `finalizeAndRedeemWithdrawRequest(B, 2Y, S)` — `_finalizeWithdraw` computes `tokensWithdrawn = totalWithdraw * 2Y / Y = 2 * totalWithdraw`.
hypotheses.impact: Vault can withdraw up to 2x (or more, by cycling) the finalized `totalWithdraw`, draining the manager's WITHDRAW_TOKEN balance and leaving other accounts unable to redeem.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track per-account yieldTokenAmount against the tokenized request's `totalYieldTokenAmount` and revert if the sum would exceed it; or disallow tokenizing into an account that already holds a request with the same requestId.
